title: Seaspawn
html_source:
A neologism that echoes Stephen’s obsession with sex as he sees what the sea has washed up as its ‘spawn’.

Possibly a reference to Aphrodite. who was supposed to have been born from the ‘sea-foam’. At any rate, the compound noun ‘seaspawn’ measures up to the chapter’s title of ‘Proteus’: a new word is made by fusing two others together; and ‘spawn’ (or perhaps ‘sperm’ in conjunction) suggests a stage of beign whose purpose lies in transforming into something else. Considering the opening concern with vision and perception, there is also quite possibly a pun on ‘sea’ and ‘see’: I see, I see, we all see the seaspawn).
